explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) passes ANTERIOR to the point where the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli meets its attached margin. The trochlear nerve passes AT this point. This anatomical landmark is important in herniation syndromes.
keyConcept: CN III passes anterior to tentorial notch; CN IV crosses at the tentorial edge.
modelAnswer: Oculomotor nerve (CN III). It passes anterior to the point where the free margin meets the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli. This is relevant to tentorial herniation where CN III can be compressed against the tentorial edge.

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to pass through the tentorial notch - it crosses between the free and attached margins of the tentorium at the point of their crossing. It is the most dorsal cranial nerve.
keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve that crosses at the tentorial notch.
modelAnswer: Trochlear nerve (CN IV). It is the only cranial nerve that passes at the point of crossing of the free and attached margins of the tentorium cerebelli. CN IV has the longest intracranial course and decussates before emerging from the dorsal midbrain.

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone. It supplies all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus, supplied by cranial part of accessory nerve via vagus).
keyConcept: CN XII passes through hypoglossal canal. Nerve to mylohyoid and anterior digastric branch of V3.
modelAnswer: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). It passes through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone to supply the muscles of the tongue.

explanation: The cerebral part of the internal carotid artery (ICA) gives off: ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery, and terminates as anterior and middle cerebral arteries. These supply the brain and orbit.
keyConcept: Cerebral ICA branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior cerebral, middle cerebral.
modelAnswer: Ophthalmic artery (to orbit), posterior communicating artery (to posterior circulation), anterior choroidal artery (to choroid plexus and optic tract), and terminates as anterior and middle cerebral arteries (to cerebral hemispheres).

explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly by the superior temporal line and inferiorly by the zygomatic arch. It contains the temporalis muscle and is continuous with the infratemporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch.
keyConcept: Temporal fossa: superior temporal line to zygomatic arch. Temporalis muscle is the key content.
modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior temporal line of the skull. Inferiorly: zygomatic arch. The temporal fossa is the space between these boundaries, containing the temporalis muscle, temporal fascia, and deep temporal arteries.

explanation: The infratemporal fossa is bounded laterally by the ramus of mandible, medially by the lateral pterygoid plate, anteriorly by the posterior surface of maxilla, posteriorly by the styloid process, and superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid.
keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: lateral = mandibular ramus, medial = pterygoid plate, anterior = maxilla, posterior = styloid, superior = sphenoid.
modelAnswer: Laterally: ramus of mandible. Medially: lateral pterygoid plate. Anteriorly: posterior surface of maxilla. Posteriorly: styloid process. Superiorly: greater wing of sphenoid. The fossa contains muscles of mastication, vessels, and nerves.

explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates with: temporal fossa (via gap deep to zygomatic arch), middle cranial fossa (foramen ovale and spinosum), orbit (inferior orbital fissure), and pterygopalatine fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure).
keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa: communicates with temporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, orbit, pterygopalatine fossa.
modelAnswer: With temporal fossa through the gap deep to zygomatic arch, with middle cranial fossa through foramen ovale and foramen spinosum, with the orbit through inferior orbital fissure, and with pterygopalatine fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.

explanation: All muscles of mastication are supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3) except the medial pterygoid, which is supplied by the trunk of the mandibular nerve. The medial pterygoid also receives fibers from the nerve to tensor veli palatini.
keyConcept: Mastication muscles: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk of V3).
modelAnswer: All are supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3) except medial pterygoid, which is supplied by the trunk of the mandibular nerve directly. The anterior division supplies temporalis, masseter, and lateral pterygoid.

explanation: All muscles of mastication elevate the mandible (close the jaw) EXCEPT the lateral pterygoid, which depresses the mandible (opens the jaw). Temporalis retracts the mandible. Medial and lateral pterygoids perform side-to-side grinding movements.
keyConcept: Mastication actions: elevation by all except lateral pterygoid (depression); retraction by temporalis; side-to-side by both pterygoids.
modelAnswer: All protrude the mandible except Temporalis (which retracts). All elevate the mandible except Lateral pterygoid (which depresses). Medial and Lateral pterygoids perform side-to-side (grinding) movements. Masseter and temporalis are primarily elevators; medial pterygoid assists in elevation and protrusion.

explanation: The lateral relations of the lateral pterygoid include: ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid plexus of veins. These structures surround and limit the lateral pterygoid.
keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid laterally: mandible ramus, medial pterygoid superficial head, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus.
modelAnswer: Ramus of mandible (lateral to lateral pterygoid), superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid plexus of veins.

explanation: The medial relations of the lateral pterygoid include: deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament. These structures are medial to the lateral pterygoid muscle.
keyConcept: Medial pterygoid relations (medial): deep medial pterygoid head, tensor palati, MMA, V3 trunk, otic ganglion.
modelAnswer: Deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palatini, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament.

explanation: The three ligaments associated with the temporomandibular joint are: lateral ligament (prevents posterior displacement), stylomandibular ligament (limits excessive opening), and sphenomandibular ligament (limits excessive opening and protrusion).
keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral (temporomandibular), stylomandibular, sphenomandibular. These are accessory ligaments.
modelAnswer: Lateral ligament (strengthens the joint laterally), stylomandibular ligament (from styloid process to mandible - limits mouth opening), and sphenomandibular ligament (from spine of sphenoid to lingula of mandible - limits protrusion).

explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives off: auriculotemporal nerve (sensory to temple and ear), lingual nerve (sensory to anterior 2/3 of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
keyConcept: Posterior V3: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves. Anterior V3: muscles of mastication + buccal nerve.
modelAnswer: Auriculotemporal nerve (sensory to temple and external ear), lingual nerve (sensory to anterior 2/3 of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (sensory to lower teeth, chin; motor to mylohyoid and anterior digastric).

explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off: mylohyoid nerve (to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric before entering mandibular foramen), mental nerve (exits mental foramen to chin and lower lip), and incisive nerve (continues in mandible to anterior teeth).
keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid nerve, mental nerve, incisive nerve. These provide sensory and motor innervation.
modelAnswer: Mylohyoid nerve (motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric - branches off before entering mandibular foramen), mental nerve (sensory to chin and lower lip), and incisive nerve (sensory to anterior teeth and premolars).

explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off: meningeal nerve (dura of middle cranial fossa), two ganglionic branches (to pterygopalatine ganglion), zygomatic nerve (to orbit and temple), and posterior superior alveolar nerves (to upper molars).
keyConcept: V2 branches: meningeal, ganglionic (to pterygopalatine ganglion), zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
modelAnswer: Meningeal nerve (to dura of middle cranial fossa), two ganglionic branches (to pterygopalatine ganglion for parasympathetic), zygomatic nerve (to lateral orbit and temple), and posterior superior alveolar nerve (to upper molars and gums).

explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa boundaries are: anterior = posterior surface of maxilla, posterior = pterygoid process (lateral and medial pterygoid plates), medial = palatine bone, lateral = opens into infratemporal fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.
keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: anterior = maxilla, posterior = pterygoid process, medial = palatine bone, lateral = opens to infratemporal fossa.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: posterior surface of maxilla. Posteriorly: pterygoid process (lateral and medial pterygoid plates). Medially: palatine bone. Laterally: opens into infratemporal fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.

explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa contains: the third part of the maxillary artery (giving off all terminal branches), the maxillary nerve (V2) with its branches, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (parasympathetic ganglion).
keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: 3rd part maxillary artery, V2, pterygopalatine ganglion.
modelAnswer: Third part of maxillary artery (terminal portion with all its branches), maxillary nerve (V2) giving off ganglionic branches, and pterygopalatine ganglion (parasympathetic ganglion receiving V2 input).

explanation: The third (terminal) part of the maxillary artery gives off: posterior superior alveolar artery, infraorbital artery, greater and lesser palatine arteries, sphenopalatine artery (to nasal cavity), pharyngeal artery, and artery of pterygoid canal.
keyConcept: 3rd maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine (greater/lesser), sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal.
modelAnswer: Posterior superior alveolar artery (to upper molars), infraorbital artery (to infraorbital region), greater and lesser palatine arteries (to palate), sphenopalatine artery (to nasal cavity), pharyngeal artery (to nasopharynx), and artery of pterygoid canal.

explanation: The pterygoid plexus of veins drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. The pterygoid plexus receives blood from muscles of mastication and surrounding structures.
keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein → retromandibular vein → external jugular vein.
modelAnswer: Maxillary vein. The pterygoid plexus of veins drains into the maxillary vein, which unites with the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, which then drains into the external jugular vein.

explanation: The pterygoid plexus communicates with: the facial vein (via the deep facial vein), the cavernous sinus (via emissary veins through foramen ovale and spinosum), and the inferior ophthalmic vein (via a vein through the inferior orbital fissure).
keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus: communicates with facial vein, cavernous sinus, inferior ophthalmic vein.
modelAnswer: With facial vein via deep facial vein, with cavernous sinus via emissary veins, and with inferior ophthalmic vein via a vein that passes through the inferior orbital fissure. These connections allow spread of infection.

explanation: The otic ganglion is located below the foramen ovale. Its sympathetic root is from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery (from superficial petrosal nerve - from ICA plexus). Parasympathetic root is from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX, tympanic plexus, and lesser petrosal nerve. It distributes to the parotid gland.
keyConcept: Otic ganglion: below foramen ovale; sympathetic = around MMA; parasympathetic = lesser petrosal nerve (from IX); distribution = parotid.
modelAnswer: Site: below foramen ovale on medial surface of V3. Sympathetic root: from plexus around middle meningeal artery (derived from external carotid artery sympathetic plexus). Parasympathetic root: from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion. Distribution: postganglionic fibers to parotid gland.

explanation: The sympathetic roots of the three parasympathetic ganglia differ: otic ganglion has sympathetic from middle meningeal artery plexus; submandibular ganglion has sympathetic from facial artery plexus; sphenopalatine ganglion has sympathetic from deep petrosal nerve (from ICA plexus).
keyConcept: Sympathetic roots: otic = MMA plexus; submandibular = facial artery plexus; sphenopalatine = deep petrosal (ICA).
modelAnswer: Otic ganglion: sympathetic root around middle meningeal artery. Submandibular ganglion: sympathetic root around facial artery. Sphenopalatine ganglion: sympathetic root from deep petrosal nerve (around internal carotid artery).

explanation: The external jugular vein receives: anterior jugular vein (from anterior neck), transverse cervical vein (from shoulder region), suprascapular vein (from scapular region), and posterior external jugular vein (from posterior scalp and neck).
keyConcept: External jugular tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
modelAnswer: Anterior jugular vein (from anterior neck), transverse cervical vein, suprascapular vein, and posterior external jugular vein. It drains into the subclavian vein.

explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed (from medial to lateral) by: semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus anterior. These muscles form the muscular floor of the triangle.
keyConcept: Posterior triangle floor: semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, scalenus anterior.
modelAnswer: Semispinalis capitis (most medial), splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus anterior (most lateral). These muscles form the floor from medial to lateral.

explanation: The posterior triangle contains: spinal accessory nerve (motor to SCM and trapezius), roots and trunks of brachial plexus (between scalenes), cutaneous nerves of cervical plexus (great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular), subclavian vein (draining arm), and external jugular vein.
keyConcept: Posterior triangle contents: CN XI, brachial plexus roots/trunks, cervical plexus cutaneous nerves, subclavian vein, external jugular vein.
modelAnswer: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), roots and trunks of brachial plexus, cutaneous nerves of cervical plexus, subclavian vein, and external jugular vein.

explanation: The cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus are: great auricular nerve (to ear), lesser occipital nerve (to scalp behind ear), transverse cervical nerve (to anterior neck), and supraclavicular nerves (to shoulder and chest).
keyConcept: Cervical plexus cutaneous: great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular nerves.
modelAnswer: Great auricular nerve (to ear and parotid region), lesser occipital nerve (to scalp behind ear), transverse cervical nerve (to anterior and lateral neck), and supraclavicular nerves (to skin over shoulder and upper chest).

explanation: The anterior triangle is bounded: anteriorly by the anterior median line of neck, posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, and superiorly by the inferior border of mandible and a line from the angle of mandible to the mastoid process.
keyConcept: Anterior triangle: anterior = midline neck, posterior = SCM, superior = mandible to mastoid.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: anterior median line of neck. Posteriorly: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle. Superiorly: inferior border of mandible and a line joining the angle of mandible to the mastoid process.

explanation: The submental triangle has: base = body of hyoid bone, apex = symphysis menti (chin), and sides = anterior bellies of both digastric muscles. The floor is formed by the two mylohyoid muscles meeting in the midline.
keyConcept: Submental triangle: base = hyoid, apex = symphysis menti, sides = anterior bellies of digastric, floor = mylohyoid muscles.
modelAnswer: Base: hyoid bone. Apex: symphysis menti (chin). On each side: anterior belly of digastric muscle. Floor: two mylohyoid muscles meeting at the midline raphe.

explanation: The submental triangle contains: submental lymph nodes (draining chin and central lower lip), submental artery and vein, small veins uniting to form the anterior jugular vein, and the mylohyoid nerve and vessels.
keyConcept: Submental triangle: submental LN, submental vessels, anterior jugular tributaries, mylohyoid nerve.
modelAnswer: Submental lymph nodes, submental artery and vein, small veins that unite to form the anterior jugular vein, and mylohyoid nerve and vessels.

explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries: anteriorly = anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly = posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, superiorly = inferior border of mandible to mastoid. The roof is skin, superficial fascia, and deep fascia. The floor is mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior = anterior digastric, posterior = posterior digastric + stylohyoid, superior = mandible, floor = mylohyoid + hyoglossus.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: anterior belly of digastric. Posteriorly: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid. Superiorly: inferior border of mandible and a line from angle of mandible to mastoid process. Roof: skin, superficial fascia, investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Floor: mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.

explanation: The digastric triangle contains: submandibular gland (major content), submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (on the gland), facial artery (grooving the gland), and facial vein (superficial to the gland).
keyConcept: Digastric triangle: submandibular gland, submandibular LN, submandibular ganglion, facial artery, facial vein.
modelAnswer: Submandibular gland (the main content), submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion, facial artery (pierces the gland), and facial vein.

explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded: superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric, anteriorly by the superior belly of omohyoid, and posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The floor is formed by hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and the constrictor muscles.
keyConcept: Carotid triangle: superior = posterior digastric, anterior = superior omohyoid, posterior = SCM, floor = hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, constrictors.
modelAnswer: Superiorly: posterior belly of digastric. Anteriorly: superior belly of omohyoid. Posteriorly: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Roof: skin, superficial fascia, investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Floor: hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and middle and inferior constrictors of the pharynx.

explanation: The carotid triangle contains the common carotid artery (CCA), internal carotid artery (ICA), and external carotid artery (ECA), along with their branches. The bifurcation of the CCA occurs in this triangle.
keyConcept: Carotid triangle: contains CCA, ICA, ECA. Bifurcation and carotid sinus/body are here.
modelAnswer: Common carotid artery (CCA), internal carotid artery (ICA), and external carotid artery (ECA). The carotid bifurcation occurs in this triangle, along with the carotid sinus and carotid body.

explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid muscles (strap muscles): sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid. These muscles attach the hyoid bone to the larynx, sternum, and scapula.
keyConcept: Muscular triangle: contains infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid).
modelAnswer: Infrahyoid muscles including sternohyoid (from sternum to hyoid), sternothyroid (from sternum to thyroid cartilage), thyrohyoid (from thyroid cartilage to hyoid), and omohyoid (from scapula to hyoid).

explanation: All infrahyoid muscles are supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) EXCEPT the thyrohyoid, which is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before branching off to supply it.
keyConcept: Infrahyoid: ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid (C1 via CN XII).
modelAnswer: All infrahyoid muscles are supplied by ansa cervicalis (C1-C3 fibers) except thyrohyoid, which is supplied by C1 fibers that accompany the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before descending to supply it.

explanation: The suprahyoid muscles have different innervation: anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid are supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (branch of V3), posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid by the facial nerve (CN VII) directly, and geniohyoid by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
keyConcept: Suprahyoid: anterior digastric + mylohyoid = V3 (mylohyoid nerve); posterior digastric + stylohyoid = CN VII; geniohyoid = C1 via CN XII.
modelAnswer: Anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid by the nerve to mylohyoid (branch of V3). Posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid by the facial nerve (CN VII). Geniohyoid by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve.

explanation: The ansa cervicalis consists of two limbs: superior limb = C1 fibers that join CN XII, then leave it and descend in front of the carotid sheath; inferior limb = fibers from C2 and C3 that descend separately to join the superior limb.
keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis: superior limb = C1 via CN XII; inferior limb = C2-C3. Both join to form the loop.
modelAnswer: It is formed of two limbs: superior limb contains fibers from C1 that initially join the hypoglossal nerve, then leave it and descend in front of the carotid sheath. Inferior limb contains fibers from C2 and C3 that descend separately to join the superior limb, forming the ansa loop.

explanation: The three cervical sympathetic ganglia are located at specific vertebral levels: superior cervical ganglion at C2-C3, middle cervical ganglion at C6-C7, and inferior cervical ganglion at C7 (often fused with T1 to form the stellate ganglion).
keyConcept: Cervical sympathetic ganglia: superior = C2-3, middle = C6-7, inferior = C7 (stellate with T1).
modelAnswer: Superior cervical ganglion: at level of C2-C3 vertebrae. Middle cervical ganglion: at level of C6-C7 vertebrae. Inferior cervical ganglion: at level of C7 vertebra (often fused with first thoracic ganglion to form stellate ganglion).

explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives off: tympanic branch (to middle ear and meninges), carotid branch (to carotid body and sinus), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar branches (to tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue).
keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular (stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, lingual.
modelAnswer: Tympanic branch (to middle ear and mastoid air cells), carotid branch (to carotid sinus and body), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus muscle), tonsillar branches (to palatine tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue for taste and general sensation).
